reason_case1_scene: An adult coworker collapses. They do not respond and are not breathing normally. You are alone, with your phone in your pocket. Help has not been called.
reason_case1_key: Unresponsive and not breathing normally; your phone is within reach.
reason_case1_context: The collapse happened in an office.
reason_case1_guess: They must have a known heart condition.
reason_case1_why: Call 911 on speaker, then immediately start CPR and follow the dispatcher. Lay rescuers use responsiveness and breathing to recognize cardiac arrest; do not delay for a pulse check.
reason_case1_transfer: If a helper is present, direct them to call 911 and get an AED while you start CPR.
reason_case2_title: A child pulled from a pool
reason_case2_scene: A 7-year-old has been safely removed from a backyard pool and is unresponsive and not breathing. You are an adult trained in CPR with breaths. No helper or phone is within reach; you would have to leave to call.
reason_case2_key: Unresponsive after drowning; calling would require leaving them.
reason_case2_context: The pool is in a backyard.
reason_case2_guess: Water must be drained from their lungs before care.
reason_case2_why: Begin CPR with rescue breaths as trained. When alone without a phone, give about 2 minutes of care before leaving to call 911. Breaths are especially important after drowning.
reason_case2_transfer: With a phone at hand, use speakerphone to call while giving care. With a helper, send them to call and get an AED. Never put yourself in danger entering water.
reason_case3_scene: A person is awake with blood rapidly flowing from a deep thigh wound. A helper is calling 911. Gloves and a dressing are beside you; a tourniquet is not yet available.
reason_case3_key: Blood is flowing rapidly; a helper is already calling 911.
reason_case3_context: The injury happened on a playing field.
reason_case3_guess: Being awake means the bleeding can wait.
reason_case3_why: Use the gloves and press firmly on the wound with the dressing. Keep pressure on. For life-threatening limb bleeding, use a manufactured tourniquet when available if trained; maintain pressure until it is ready.
reason_case3_transfer: Severe blood loss can occur without spurting or bright-red blood. Look at the amount and flow, and keep watching for changes.
reason_case4_scene: A responsive adult at dinner cannot speak, cough, or breathe. Another person is calling 911. The adult is not pregnant, and you can reach around their abdomen.
reason_case4_key: They are responsive but cannot speak, cough, or breathe.
reason_case4_context: They are standing beside a dinner table.
reason_case4_guess: A drink will wash the food down.
reason_case4_why: Give 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts, repeating until the blockage clears or they become unresponsive. The inability to cough or speak signals severe choking.
reason_case4_transfer: If they can cough forcefully, encourage coughing and monitor. If they become unresponsive, lower them safely and start CPR as trained. Choking care differs for infants and pregnancy.
reason_case5_scene: A helper is doing CPR on an unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally. EMS has been called. You arrive with an AED and can attach its pads while the helper continues compressions.
reason_case5_key: CPR is underway and an AED is now available.
reason_case5_context: The AED has just been taken out of its case.
reason_case5_guess: Every person receiving CPR will need a shock.
reason_case5_why: Turn on the AED, apply its pads, and follow its prompts. Keep compressions going during setup where possible. Everyone must be clear during analysis and any shock; immediately resume CPR when prompted.
reason_case5_transfer: An AED may say no shock is advised. That does not mean the person has recovered: follow its prompt to resume CPR.
reason_case6_scene: A student has stopped having a seizure. They are unresponsive but breathing normally. A helper is speaking with 911. No head, neck, or back injury is suspected.
reason_case6_key: The seizure has stopped; breathing is normal and no spinal injury is suspected.
reason_case6_guess: They need something put into their mouth.
reason_case6_why: Place them on their side in the recovery position and monitor breathing. Put nothing in their mouth. Follow the dispatcher while help is coming.
reason_case6_transfer: If breathing stops or becomes only gasping, the priority changes to CPR and an AED. Do not assume someone is simply sleeping after a seizure.
reason_case7_scene: A neighbor suddenly has slurred speech, one side of their face droops, and one arm is weak. You saw the symptoms begin 15 minutes ago. No one has called for help.
reason_case7_key: The speech, face, and arm changes began suddenly.
reason_case7_guess: Symptoms must persist for an hour before calling.
reason_case7_why: Call 911 for possible stroke and report when symptoms began. These signs need emergency assessment even if they improve. Do not wait to confirm a diagnosis.
reason_case7_transfer: Sudden balance or vision changes can also be stroke warnings. You do not need every sign before calling.
reason_case8_scene: An adult has persistent chest pressure, feels sweaty, and reports discomfort in their arm. They are awake and breathing. They suggest waiting to see if it passes.
reason_case8_key: Persistent chest pressure with sweating and arm discomfort.
reason_case8_context: They are able to describe their symptoms.
reason_case8_guess: Someone who can speak cannot be having a heart attack.
reason_case8_why: Call 911 for possible heart attack. Stay with them and follow the dispatcher. Being awake does not make these warning signs safe to wait out.
reason_case8_transfer: Symptoms vary. Shortness of breath, nausea, or discomfort in the back or jaw can also occur; chest pain need not be crushing.
reason_case9_scene: An adult is unresponsive but breathing normally. No head, neck, or back injury is suspected. A helper has called 911 and is following the dispatcher. You are beside the person.
reason_case9_key: Breathing is normal, with no suspected spinal injury; help has been called.
reason_case9_guess: No visible injury means they do not need help.
reason_case9_why: Use the recovery position and keep checking breathing and responsiveness. It helps protect their airway while help is coming. Unresponsiveness still requires emergency care.
reason_case9_transfer: If a head, neck, or back injury is suspected, leave them as found unless movement is needed for safety, CPR, or bleeding control. Follow the dispatcher.
reason_case10_scene: An adult with asthma is struggling to breathe and cannot speak in full sentences. Their rescue inhaler is empty. They are awake, sitting forward. Help has not been called.
reason_case10_key: Severe breathing difficulty and no usable rescue inhaler.
reason_case10_context: They are sitting in a chair.
reason_case10_guess: They should walk around to improve their breathing.
reason_case10_why: Call 911 and follow the dispatcher. Let them stay in a position that makes breathing easier, and monitor for changes. Do not delay help to look for another inhaler.
reason_case10_transfer: If their own prescribed reliever is available, help them use it as trained. Severe or worsening breathing difficulty still needs urgent help.
reason_intro_title: Find the clue. Choose the action.
reason_intro_text: Connect what you observe to the next helpful action in 10 short scenes. Take time to reason; there is no timer.
reason_invalid: This saved practice cannot be resumed. Start a fresh set; your practice record is still available.
reason_notice_body: Pick the observation that matters most. Separate evidence from background details and guesses.
reason_decide_body: Use the people, phone, and equipment described. Some tasks can happen at the same time.
reason_explain_body: Read the reasoning, compare a changed situation, then revisit the decisions that needed support.
reason_context: Practice role: an adult helper with the training stated in each scene. Scene safety has already been checked. In a real emergency, get help and give care within your training.
reason_review_body: The first check shows what you chose before correction. A supported decision is a useful next practice target.
reason_reflect_title: Try it in your own words
reason_reflect: Choose one scene. Explain: “I noticed ___, so I would ___ because ___.” Then change one detail and explain whether your action changes. You can speak, sign, write, or discuss with a partner.
reason_limit: This record describes decisions in a practice activity. Hands-on training and certification assess practical skills.
reason_no_timer: Take your time · No speed score
reason_scene_safe: Scene safety is already checked. Choose the key clue and your next action using the details above.
reason_select_both: Select one clue and one action to check your reasoning.
reason_hint_guide: Use this clue to choose an action. This round will be recorded as supported practice.
reason_cue_feedback: Choose an observed condition that changes the care needed, together with any help or equipment already available.
reason_action_feedback: Re-read who is already helping and what is happening now. Choose the action you can take next.
reason_cue_right: Your clue identifies the key condition. Now connect it to the next action.
reason_action_right: Your action fits this scene. Choose the clue that explains why.
reason_record_intro: A reasoned decision means the key clue and action were both correct on the first check, without a hint. Repeated practice builds familiarity; this record does not measure emergency readiness.
reason_legacy_body: Your previous action-only result is preserved. The updated activity also checks the observation behind the action.
reason_record_saved: Completed practice records are saved on this device. A session can be resumed while you move between lab activities.
reason_menu_record_desc: See clue-and-action connections, supported practice, and scenes to revisit.
reason_menu_sleuth_desc: Connect the key observation to your next action in 10 scenes. Get coaching and revisit missed decisions.
reason_call_def: Call 911 and follow the dispatcher. In Maine, text 911 if you cannot make a voice call.
reason_cpr_def: For unresponsiveness with absent or abnormal breathing. Give CPR as trained; breaths matter especially for children and drowning.
reason_aed_def: Turn on, attach pads, follow prompts. Everyone clear during analysis and shock; promptly resume CPR.
reason_pressure_def: Press firmly on the wound with a dressing or cloth. Use gloves if available and maintain pressure.
reason_choking_def: For severe choking in a responsive adult or child: 5 back blows, then 5 thrusts. Technique varies by age and pregnancy.
reason_recovery_def: For unresponsiveness with normal breathing and no suspected spinal injury. Position on their side and monitor.
